one_liner: Microsoft Research C library for FourQ ECDH and SchnorrQ signatures; up to 5.6x faster scalar multiplication than fast P-256 code.
what_it_does: Implements the FourQ curve, a twisted Edwards curve over GF((2^127-1)^2) with a 246-bit prime-order subgroup and cofactor 392. It provides cofactor ECDH with 32-byte compressed or 64-byte uncompressed public keys, SchnorrQ signatures (EdDSA-style, 32-byte keys, 64-byte signatures, SHA-512) and, in the portable build only, hash-to-curve. The C API in FourQ_api.h also exposes the raw primitives ecc_mul, ecc_mul_fixed and ecc_mul_double, plus arithmetic modulo the curve order. It does not replace P-256: the curve, key formats and encodings are all different, and every call returns an ECCRYPTO_STATUS code.
how_it_is_fast: FourQ has two cheap endomorphisms, psi (from the Q-curve construction) and phi (from complex multiplication with discriminant -40), which allow a four-dimensional GLV decomposition of a 256-bit scalar into four 64-bit sub-scalars. After a constant-time recoding (the Faz-Hernandez/Longa/Sanchez GLV-GLS recoding), variable-base multiplication is 64 double-and-add steps over an 8-point table, using complete extended twisted Edwards formulas over the Mersenne prime 2^127-1, where reduction is very cheap. Fixed-base multiplication uses an LSB-set comb with an 80-point (7.5 KB) table, and verification uses interleaved wNAF with a 24 KB table. On x64 Linux the GF(p^2) arithmetic is hand-written assembly, whose AVX2 variant also uses MULX and ymm registers.
when_to_use: You control both ends of the protocol (internal RPC, a device fleet, a research prototype) and want the fastest constant-time ECDH or signatures at the 128-bit security level, with no standards requirement.

Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman on x64 Linux, where scalar multiplication dominates the cost. The paper reports 30-40k cycles for fixed-base key generation and 50-72k cycles for variable-base multiplication on Broadwell through Sandy Bridge.
32-bit ARM, NEON (Cortex-A7/A8/A9/A15) or Cortex-M4 targets, which have their own tuned code trees that share the same API.

Benchmarking or teaching endomorphism-accelerated ECC: the code is compact, comes with Magma scripts that check the paper's operation counts, and can be built with or without the endomorphisms (USE_ENDO).
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs interop or compliance, such as TLS, X.509, SSH, JOSE/COSE or FIPS 140. FourQ is not a NIST or IETF curve, and the Curve4Q Internet-Draft (draft-ladd-cfrg-4q-01) expired in 2017.
macOS or any OS other than Linux or Windows. FourQ.h stops with #error "Unsupported OS" unless __LINUX__ or __WINDOWS__ is defined, and the Mac issues #2 and #6 are unanswered.

Production use without your own validation. Open issue #10 (2024) reports that the GF(p^2) inversion test FAILS with GCC 11.4.1 at -O2/-O3 while clang 15 passes, and nobody from the project has replied.
SchnorrQ over large or streamed messages. Sign and Verify calloc a full copy of the message (SizeMessage+64 bytes, length typed as unsigned int), and there is no prehash or streaming API.
Hardened embedded deployments using the bundled side-channel tree as-is: FourQ_ARM_side_channel is labeled experimental and 'DO NOT USE AS IS IN PRODUCTION', and its SHA-512 is not DPA-protected.

integration.form: source-drop (the makefile builds the test binaries, and libFourQ.so with SHARED_LIB=TRUE; a Visual Studio 2015 solution builds FourQ.lib; no install target, CMake or pkg-config)
integration.dependencies: None external. Bundled public-domain SHA-512 and a /dev/urandom or BCryptGenRandom/RtlGenRandom RNG, both replaceable via macros in FourQ.h. The Cortex-M4 trees bundle libopencm3 (LGPL-3.0) and CC0 STM32 wrappers.
integration.min_toolchain: C with 128-bit integers (GCC/clang mode(TI)) or MSVC _umul128. Tested with Visual Studio 2015, GCC 4.9 and clang 3.8; GCC 11.4.1 at -O2/-O3 is reported to fail the fp tests. The makefile uses GNU sed -i.
integration.platforms: Linux and Windows only. x64 has the optimized path (the default AVX2 assembly needs Haswell+ with BMI2 MULX, and assembly is Linux-only, so Windows gets the C path). ARMv8 64-bit has optimized C; x86 and 32-bit ARM use the portable C. ARMv6/ARMv7, NEON and Cortex-M4 have separate trees.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Operations keep their state on the stack and read constant tables, but the Linux RNG lazily opens a static /dev/urandom descriptor with no locking, so concurrent first calls race.

gotchas: ecc_mul takes a clear_cofactor flag. The high-level SecretAgreement calls clear the cofactor (x392) and reject a neutral-point result, but raw ecc_mul callers must pass true for any untrusted point. The ECDH output is only the 32-byte y-coordinate.

The default Linux build adds -march=native (EXTENDED_SET) and, on x64, AVX2+MULX assembly, so the binaries are not portable. Set EXTENDED_SET=FALSE and AVX2=FALSE (or GENERIC=TRUE) for distributable builds.

TEMP_ZEROING is commented out by default, so secret intermediates in scalar multiplication are not wiped. ecc_mul_double (used for verification) and point validation are explicitly non-constant-time and meant only for public inputs.

SchnorrQ signatures always end in a 0x00 byte because s < 2^246, and the verifier rejects anything else (issue #3). Secret keys are unclamped 256-bit hash outputs, and nonces are deterministic, as in EdDSA.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose FourQlib over the SUPERCOP Ed25519 code or ENG25519 only when you do not need Ed25519/X25519 compatibility and your CPUs lack AVX-512 IFMA. Its 2015 paper measured 2.2-2.9x faster variable-base multiplication than the Curve25519 code of that era, whereas ENG25519 speeds up the standard curves on IFMA hardware. Use libsecp256k1 for Bitcoin's secp256k1 and ocaml-curve448 if you need X448/Ed448.
verified_claims_summary: In Table 5 of the ASIACRYPT 2015 paper (ePrint 2015/565), FourQlib 2.0 did a variable-base scalar multiplication in 72k cycles on a Sandy Bridge i7-2600 and 56k on a Haswell i7-4770 (TurboBoost off), against 400k and 312k for the Gueron-Krasnov P-256 code (about 5.6x), and one ephemeral DH round in 112k vs 490k cycles (4.4x). The P-256 figures were copied from the Gueron-Krasnov paper rather than re-run, no compiler or flags are given, the FourQ code then used no vector instructions, and the current v3.1 code has not been re-benchmarked against a baseline.
status_note: Abandoned: the last code change was the hash-to-curve addition on 2021-03-19, the last commit (2022-08-31) only added Microsoft's SECURITY.md, and there has never been a tagged release (issue #1). The MIT core is small enough to vendor, but plan on validating your own compiler and maintaining fixes yourself.
